intro_detail: I make games, I’m interested in AI and I like 3D rendering.
selection_note: Cards to collect, gravity to explore and plants grown through code.
home_booster_description: Open packs, trade cards and play duels, with WebGL effects that bring each pack opening to life.
home_spellwar_description: A C++ and OpenGL engine where the character’s frame of reference changes when moving between platforms.
home_plants_description: Rewriting rules that grow plants in 3D, with an editor for trying out different forms.
projects_intro: Personal projects and work from my studies. Games, web applications, 3D rendering and AI applied to physics.
spellwar_summary: A 3D game with a custom engine in C++ and OpenGL.
spellwar_detail: SpellWar is a third-person 3D game built around floating platforms and a C++ and OpenGL engine. This academic project brings together graphics programming, geometry and movement mechanics.
spellwar_focus: The game is a testing ground for a complete engine: scenes, camera, animation, collisions, world generation and PBR rendering. The work covers both the underlying systems and what appears on screen.
plants_summary: Plants generated using L-systems, with 3D rendering in WebGL.
plants_detail: This project started with reading The Algorithmic Beauty of Plants (ABOP). It was mainly about studying the ideas and putting them into practice.
plants_focus: Turn rewriting rules into 3D geometry, then explore the result with a WebGL renderer, a camera and editable parameters.
eyefox_summary: An Android puzzle developed during my studies.
eyefox_detail: The goal is to make two grids match. Changing a tile’s colour also changes its neighbours.
eyefox_focus: Build a puzzle around this rule and make it work on a phone.

booster_summary: Pokémon packs to open, cards to collect and trade.
booster_detail: Booster Break is a personal project that colleagues also contribute to. You can browse your collection, trade cards and prepare three-Pokémon duels. There is also a sandbox for opening packs without an account, just for fun.
booster_focus: The cards and pack-opening effects use WebGL. Behind them, a TypeScript app with React, an Elysia API and a PostgreSQL database handles collections, trades and duels. The project keeps growing through new ideas and contributions.
pinnacle_summary: Exploring activation regions in physics-informed neural networks.
pinnacle_detail: PINNacle is the starting point for this group project on explaining PINNs, neural networks trained to satisfy physical equations. The idea is to examine how their activations partition the domain, then make that geometry visible as training progresses.
pinnacle_focus: I worked on extracting ReLU, tanh and SiLU activations, partitioning them into regions, quantile sampling and data export. I also developed parts of the C++ and OpenGL viewer, including rendering, shaders and image-sequence export. Density statistics and heatmaps are part of the group’s work.
pinnacle_visual_caption: An activation-region rendering from our defense presentation, in the sequence showing their evolution over 20,000 epochs. This is a still image.
dit_summary: Two image generation experiments: a StyleGAN-inspired GAN and a latent diffusion transformer.
dit_detail: This academic project explores 256 × 256 image generation with two compact PyTorch models. The GAN generates landscapes from noise. Cheap DiT learns to denoise representations of paintings in a VAE’s latent space, then converts them back into images.
dit_focus: I worked on model architecture and training. For diffusion, I moved from pixel space to latent space to reduce the sequence length processed by the transformer. The results retain visible limitations: sometimes blurry shapes, imperfect reconstructions and repeating patterns in the GAN outputs.

journey_intro: From software back to maths, following the thread of projects and experiences.
journey_engineering_body: A three-year engineering programme with foundations in algorithms, mathematics and software engineering, followed by a specialisation in image, sound and artificial intelligence. The track covers machine learning, deep learning, image and audio analysis, image synthesis and virtual reality. I put these ideas into practice through projects in games, 3D rendering, image generation and neural network explainability.
journey_work_body: At Galadrim, I designed and built custom applications from established business requirements, from technical architecture to production deployment. Working in an Agile environment, I collaborated with clients to present progress, clarify evolving requirements and explain technical constraints and trade-offs.
journey_work_branch_1: Agentic development: designing agent skills and workflows for scoping, architecture, implementation, review and validation, to accelerate development while keeping control of quality.
journey_work_branch_2: Technical guidance and mentoring: supporting developers, guiding implementation decisions and reviewing code.
journey_engineering_school: ENSICAEN · Image, sound and artificial intelligence
journey_work_employer: Galadrim · Internship from February to August, then a permanent role from August 2026
journey_work_branch_3: Delivery and reliability: cloud infrastructure, CI/CD, deployments, testing and monitoring, with attention to performance and costs.
journey_work_branch_4: My work includes an automotive parts e-commerce platform built from scratch on AWS, and gamification features for a shopping centre platform.
journey_cs_body: A year focused on computer science after my first year in mathematics, before joining the engineering programme at ENSICAEN.
journey_math_body: A first year at university focused on mathematics, the starting point of my path into computer science.

home_research_body: I enjoy building an image as much as understanding how it emerges. These two projects explore neural networks from different angles: generating images and looking at how a model partitions a physics problem.
home_dit_note: From noise to images, with actual training outputs
home_pinnacle_note: Making a network’s activation regions visible
plants_grammar_body: An L-system starts with an axiom, a string of symbols. At each generation, rules replace those symbols with new sequences. For the plant models, repeating these rules produces an increasingly branching structure.
plants_turtle_body: A 3D turtle then interprets the string: move forward, rotate, draw a segment, save a position and return to it to start a branch. The project turns these instructions into geometry, then displays it with its WebGL renderer.
plants_plant_alt: Green WebGL rendering of the branching plant preset
plants_tree_alt: WebGL rendering of a tree with brown branches and green leaves
plants_tree_caption: Branching tree · 7 generations · Branches and leaves come from the same grammar
plants_forms_body: Rules can describe more than trees. The flowering plant combines stems, leaves and petals; the Hilbert curve uses 90° turns to fill space. These four renders come from the presets in the explorer above, using their original parameters.
plants_flower_alt: WebGL plant with brown stems, green leaves and red flowers
plants_flower_caption: Flowering plant · 5 generations · Three colours for the different parts
plants_hilbert_alt: Red 3D Hilbert curve forming a network of right-angle segments
plants_experiment_body: The editor lets you change the axiom, rules, generation count, angles and colours, then redraw the scene. Camera and lighting controls help reveal the volumes. Shapes can also be exported as OBJ/MTL or PLY for use in another 3D tool.
plants_limits_body: The result is geometry built from deterministic rules, rather than a simulation of biological growth. Generation counts and geometry size are bounded to keep exploration usable in the browser.
booster_story_opening_title: The pleasure of opening a pack
booster_story_opening_p1: Choose an expansion, open a pack, reveal the cards one by one: the app brings this small collector’s ritual to the browser. The collection then lets you find a card by name, expansion or rarity, and keep track of duplicates.
booster_story_opening_p2: A sandbox gives access to older packs without creating an account. The cards are not saved: you can simply try the opening sequence and see the result. The screenshots below come from the app, including a Silver Tempest demo draw.
booster_story_packs_alt: Booster Break interface showing a 3D Pitch Black pack and the expansion picker
booster_story_packs_caption: Choosing an expansion in the public app, before signing in
booster_story_recap_alt: Summary of the ten cards drawn from a Silver Tempest pack in the sandbox
booster_story_recap_caption: A sandbox draw, with no cards added to a collection
booster_story_duels_title: Trade cards and play your collection
booster_story_duels_p1: The cards are also a way to play with others. The trading area lets players list a card, receive offers and choose one. Surcharge duels use three Pokémon from your collection, with a total power limit when building your team.
booster_story_duels_p2: Each player has five energy points for the whole duel. In every round, both players secretly choose a card and how much energy to commit, then reveal their choices together. You have to spread your strength across at most three rounds; the cards stay in your collection. Elo rankings and statistics keep track of the matches.
booster_story_duels_alt: Grid of Pokémon cards from the Nuit Noire expansion, grouped by rarity in Booster Break
booster_story_duels_caption: Public preview of the Nuit Noire expansion, available without an account
booster_story_webgl_p1: The renderer does more than display an image. A WebGL mesh deforms the wrapper as it tears open. For cards, shaders combine the artwork, material textures and masks to put reflections in the right areas. Different finish profiles give holographic cards their appearance.
booster_story_webgl_p2: Tilting a card changes its lighting and reflections as you inspect it. These effects are a visual layer: the API handles collections, trades and duel results.
booster_story_foil_alt: A large Zygarde card reveal with coloured reflections across its holographic finish
booster_story_foil_caption: The ninth card from the same draw, with its finish rendered in WebGL
pinnacle_story_method_p1: With ReLU, a given combination of active neurons defines a region where the network is affine. PyTorch hooks collect activations as points pass through the network. Points sharing the same pattern receive the same region identifier, making the partition of the input space visible.
pinnacle_story_method_p2: With tanh and SiLU, transitions are smooth, so regions need an empirical definition. We explored clustering with a first-order Taylor distance, then a quantile-based alternative for partitioning the activation distribution. Threshold selection and computational cost are as much a part of the problem as visualization.
pinnacle_story_method_alt: A ReLU network diagram whose active and inactive states form an identifier, connected to a map of colored regions
pinnacle_story_method_caption: Extraction principle, slide 11: activation patterns become region identifiers. This diagram explains the method using a small ReLU network.
pinnacle_story_viewer_p1: The exported data feeds a C++ viewer with OpenGL for rendering and ImGui for controls. It supports exploring regions in 2D and 3D, moving the camera and exporting frames to follow their evolution during training. The defense presentation includes an animation spanning 20,000 epochs.
pinnacle_story_viewer_p2: These three renderings come from the project’s results. Colors distinguish regions; they do not represent temperature or prediction error. The partitions vary considerably with the activation, with fine, closely packed regions near the center. For tanh and SiLU, these are the empirical partitions produced by the method.
pinnacle_story_relu_alt: A disk of multicolored ReLU regions, with many small polygons near the center and larger regions toward the edge
pinnacle_story_relu_caption: ReLU · Activation regions presented in the defense results, slide 32
pinnacle_story_tanh_alt: A circular tanh partition in multicolored regions, with long shapes radiating toward the edge
pinnacle_story_tanh_caption: tanh · Empirical partition presented in the defense results, slide 33
pinnacle_story_silu_alt: A SiLU partition of a disk, with a central band of very small regions and larger polygons toward the sides
pinnacle_story_silu_caption: SiLU · Empirical partition presented in the defense results, slide 34
pinnacle_story_density_p1: The group’s work adds region-density analysis to the colored views. Two approaches are presented: examining a circular neighborhood of fixed size, or starting from a fixed number of neighboring regions. The tanh maps below highlight the areas where the partition is densest.
pinnacle_story_density_p2: This view helps explore what the network represents, but it does not establish that a physical solution is more accurate. Results also depend on the region definition and density method. At the end of the project, integrating these heatmaps directly into the viewer remained a possible next step.
pinnacle_story_density_alt: Two tanh density maps side by side, using a circle method and an N-neighbor method, with their axes and distinct color scales
pinnacle_story_density_caption: Group analysis, slide 24: circle method on the left, N-neighbor method on the right. The legends use different scales, so colors cannot be compared directly between the maps.
eyefox_story_rule_p1: Two grids, light and dark tiles, and a limited number of moves to make them match. Tapping a tile flips its colour and that of its neighbours, including diagonals. A single move can change up to nine tiles, so you have to look at the surrounding pattern as well as the tile itself.
eyefox_story_rule_p2: Each puzzle starts with a randomly generated target. The game makes a copy and applies a sequence of valid moves to it. Repeating those flips returns the grid to the target, so every puzzle has a solution. Grid size and the move budget change as the levels progress.
eyefox_story_game_alt: Android screenshot of Eyefox Puzzle with two four-by-four grids, the move counter and lives
eyefox_story_game_caption: The Android game, with the target and the grid to transform
eyefox_story_android_title: From a puzzle to an Android app
eyefox_story_android_p1: The Android game adds progression, a limited number of attempts and animations to the basic rule. The current level is saved locally so players can resume their progress. In the Java code, grid and level logic are separate from the views and Android interaction handling.
eyefox_story_android_p2: The small game embedded on this page brings the rules and artwork to the browser. Its three difficulty shortcuts let you try a few puzzles. The Android campaign and its saved progression are not part of this demo.
eyefox_story_menu_alt: Pixel-art Android menu for Eyefox Puzzle, showing a fox and the current level
eyefox_story_menu_caption: The Android game’s menu and saved progression
spellwar_story_engine_title: From an engine to a playable world
spellwar_story_engine_p1: I split the code into two parts: wgame contains the engine systems, while spellwar handles characters, platforms and game rules. Window management, input, camera and scenes provide a foundation separate from the game logic.
spellwar_story_engine_p2: The prototype offers several characters and third-person exploration. Walking, running and moving between platforms bring together keyboard input, model animation, the camera and collisions.
spellwar_story_engine_alt: Armoured character facing floating platforms, red trees and purple spikes in SpellWar
spellwar_story_engine_caption: In-game capture: the character, scenery and platforms share one OpenGL scene.
spellwar_story_physics_title: Moving through a world with no fixed up
spellwar_story_physics_p1: The platforms do not all share the same orientation. To reach a surface, the player aims at it and jumps while moving from an edge. The custom physics model then adapts the character’s position and orientation to the destination platform.
spellwar_story_physics_p2: Before starting this transition, the engine checks the player’s collision box at several points along the path. An obstacle prevents the crossing. Scenery volumes are stored in a tree that subdivides space into eight regions to narrow the objects checked.
spellwar_story_physics_p3: Terrain generation places platforms with varying sizes and positions, rejecting overlaps. It then adds vegetation, rocks and spikes while checking their placement. The orientations and distances between surfaces give the world its distinctive geometry.
spellwar_story_platforms_alt: SpellWar character looking at tilted and inverted platforms in the sky
spellwar_story_platforms_caption: Surfaces with different orientations make changes to the character’s frame of reference central to movement.
spellwar_story_terrain_alt: Downward view of SpellWar floating platforms covered with rocks, trees and plants
spellwar_story_terrain_caption: The map combines generated platforms with scenery placed on their surfaces.
spellwar_story_rendering_title: Materials and light in real time
spellwar_story_rendering_p1: The PBR renderer uses each material’s base colour, roughness and metallic properties. GLSL shaders calculate diffuse and specular components from the light, the surface and the camera position.
spellwar_story_rendering_p2: Normal maps add lighting detail without adding geometry. glTF models, their animations and the space background complete the rendering pipeline. The video shows this rendering as the character moves through the world.
spellwar_story_rendering_alt: SpellWar character moving between differently oriented platforms and turning to match local gravity
spellwar_story_rendering_caption: Movement between platforms and character rotation to match local gravity. In-game footage, without audio.
